explain.say: A levee is a long earth bank built along a river to keep floodwater off the land behind it. It is made of soil rolled hard in thin layers, wide at the base and sloping on both sides.

faq.a: A levee is an embankment, usually of compacted earth, built along a river or coast to hold back high water and protect the land and towns behind it.

faq.q: Why do levees have a clay core?
faq.a: Clay has extremely tiny pores, so water seeps through it very slowly. A clay core acts as a watertight barrier inside the bank.

faq.q: What is seepage under a levee?
faq.a: During a flood, high water pressure can push water through sandy soil beneath the levee. If it bubbles up behind carrying soil, called a sand boil, it can hollow out the levee's foundation.

The main causes are water overtopping and eroding the back slope, seepage washing out soil underneath, and soaked banks sliding. In New Orleans in 2005, overtopping and weak foundations caused many failures.

faq.q: Why are levees covered in grass?
faq.a: Grass roots bind the soil surface so rain, waves and fast currents cannot wash it away. The grass is kept short so inspectors can spot cracks and animal burrows.

facts: During Hurricane Katrina in 2005, levee and floodwall failures left about 80 percent of New Orleans under water.
Sand boils, where water bubbles up behind a levee carrying soil, are a warning sign that seepage may undermine it.
